abstract: Device-independent quantum key distribution (DIQKD) can guarantee security without trusting the internal workings of the measurement devices, but extending it to fiber networks demands high-quality entanglement, reliable heralding, and faithful photon transmission simultaneously. Here, we address these requirements in an event-ready asymmetric atom-photon architecture implemented over $25\,\mathrm{km}$ of spooled telecom fiber. A single trapped $^{40}\mathrm{Ca}^{+}$ ion forms one party of the protocol while a single transmitted photon measured at the remote station forms the other. Double quantum frequency conversion and active polarization stabilization preserve the atom-photon quantum correlation across the full link. We obtain a Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt parameter of $|S|=2.75^{+0.16}_{-0.15}$, exceeding the threshold $|S|=2.362$ required for a positive asymptotic secret-key fraction under the DIQKD model used. Within the same asymptotic model, this corresponds to a conservative estimate of 69 secret-key bits out of 10908 detected Bell states. The demonstrated architecture establishes a route towards DIQKD in heterogeneous, repeater-compatible quantum networks.
one_liner: A trapped Ca+ ion and telecom photon demonstrate event-ready DIQKD correlations across 25 km of fiber.
why_it_matters: It is a concrete step toward device-independent QKD over heterogeneous, repeater-compatible quantum networks.
detailed_summary: The work implements an asymmetric device-independent QKD architecture in which a single trapped 40Ca+ ion is one node and a transmitted photon measured after 25 km of spooled telecom fiber is the remote node. Double quantum frequency conversion and active polarization stabilization preserve atom-photon correlations across the link. The experiment reports |S|=2.75 with asymmetric uncertainty, exceeding the stated DIQKD threshold of |S|=2.362, and estimates 69 asymptotic secret-key bits from 10908 detected Bell states under its model.
platform_or_system: trapped 40Ca+ ion linked to a telecom photon
main_result: The system achieves event-ready atom-photon Bell correlations over 25 km with |S|=2.75 and a positive asymptotic DIQKD key estimate.
application_angle: The architecture points toward secure quantum-network links combining stationary matter qubits, telecom transmission, and future repeater nodes.

title: Universal Fidelity Law for Linear-Optical Entangling Gates
abstract: Imperfect photon sources degrade the performance of interference-based linear-optical entangling gates. We derive a universal fidelity law for these gates in terms of two standard source metrics: Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility and second-order coherence. We model the multiphoton component as an arbitrary overlap between noise and signal photons. While different values of the signal-noise overlap produce different error structures, associated with different physical platforms, all result in the same fidelity law. We test the model on our actively synchronized CNOT-gate experiment and against published results across different platforms, with no free parameters. This framework turns source characterization into a unified benchmark for photonic quantum computing.
one_liner: A universal law links linear-optical entangling-gate fidelity to HOM visibility and g2 source quality.
why_it_matters: It turns standard photon-source measurements into a platform-independent benchmark for photonic quantum gates.
detailed_summary: The paper derives a fidelity law for interference-based linear-optical entangling gates using two common photon-source metrics: Hong-Ou-Mandel visibility and second-order coherence. The model allows arbitrary overlap between multiphoton noise and signal photons, producing platform-dependent error structures but the same final fidelity relation. The authors test the law on an actively synchronized CNOT-gate experiment and published cross-platform data with no free parameters.
main_result: A no-free-parameter fidelity law predicts linear-optical entangling-gate performance from HOM visibility and g2 across platforms.
application_angle: The framework can standardize source and gate benchmarking for photonic quantum-computing hardware development.

title: Modulating Retroreflector-Aided UAV-Based FSO/QKD Systems
abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs)-based free-space optics (FSO)/quantum key distribution (QKD) systems require high-precision pointing mechanisms. This increases system complexity and limits rapid deployment for lightweight and energy-constrained UAVs. This paper proposes a modulating retroreflector (MRR)-equipped UAV architecture for BB84-QKD systems that enables simplified yet accurate tracking while relaxing pointing requirements. A realistic quantum channel model is developed, for which we newly derive the channel probability distribution of transmittance (PDT). Capitalizing on the derived channel PDT, several QKD performance metrics are analytically obtained. Numerical results verify the feasibility of the proposed MRR-aided UAV for practical QKD deployment, highlight its effectiveness over conventional UAV-ground systems, and validate the accuracy of the developed analytical framework.
one_liner: A modulating-retroreflector UAV architecture is analyzed for simpler pointing in free-space BB84 QKD links.
why_it_matters: It targets lightweight, rapidly deployable aerial QKD systems by reducing the burden of high-precision UAV pointing.
detailed_summary: The paper proposes a UAV-based free-space optics and BB84-QKD architecture using a modulating retroreflector to simplify tracking and relax pointing requirements. It develops a realistic quantum channel model and derives the probability distribution of transmittance for the link. Analytical QKD performance metrics based on this distribution are compared with numerical results, supporting feasibility and showing benefits over conventional UAV-ground configurations.
main_result: The study derives an analytical channel and QKD-performance framework showing feasible MRR-aided UAV BB84 deployment with relaxed pointing constraints.
application_angle: The architecture could make mobile, lightweight, and fast-deployable QKD nodes more practical for temporary or hard-to-reach links.

title: Dynamical, thermal, and ground-state multiparameter quantum metrology: Fundamental limits and their attainability in magnetometry
abstract: We consider the simultaneous estimation of multiple parameters in Hamiltonians of the form $H_{\vecθ}= H_{\vecθ}^P + H^C$, where $H_{\vecθ}^P$ encodes the unknown parameters and $H^C$ is a control term. We consider three basic paradigmatic frameworks for metrology: (i) dynamical, where the parameters are encoded unitarily, (ii) thermal, and (iii) ground state. We generalize previous bounds for single-parameter estimation to simultaneous multiparameter estimation for all three metrological settings and establish the conditions required for their saturability. We then focus on vector magnetometry, deriving tight bounds for the simultaneous estimation of magnetic-field components and identifying optimal many-body control Hamiltonians $H^C$ that saturate them. These results establish the fundamental limits of vector magnetometry for unitary dynamics, thermal equilibrium states, and ground states.
one_liner: Extends fundamental multiparameter metrology bounds and attainability conditions to vector magnetometry across dynamical, thermal, and ground-state regimes.
why_it_matters: It clarifies when simultaneous magnetic-field-component estimation can reach quantum limits and what many-body controls are required.
detailed_summary: The paper generalizes single-parameter quantum metrology bounds to simultaneous estimation in Hamiltonians with parameter and control terms. It treats unitary dynamics, thermal equilibrium, and ground-state sensing, deriving saturability conditions for each setting. For vector magnetometry, it identifies tight bounds for field-component estimation and optimal many-body control Hamiltonians that can attain them.
main_result: The work derives tight, saturable multiparameter bounds for vector magnetometry in dynamical, thermal, and ground-state sensing settings.
application_angle: The results provide design rules for quantum magnetometers that estimate full vector fields rather than one component at a time.

title: Effective-Hamiltonian Quantum Solvers for Differential Equations: Alternative Constructions and Function Encodings
abstract: Differential equations can be encoded as ground-state problems by constructing a positive-semidefinite effective Hamiltonian whose minimum-energy state represents the solution. We extend this framework in several directions. First, we show how multiple nonzero initial, boundary, and data conditions can be incorporated into the homogeneous formulation $A | f\rangle=0$ using a known nonzero reference condition. We then analyse an alternative formulation based on $A |f\rangle = | b\rangle$, with Hamiltonian $H_b=A^\dagger(I-|b\rangle\langle b|)A$, which incorporates source terms and nonzero constraints through an augmented system. For nonlinear differential equations, we examine the unphysical ground-state degeneracy introduced by tensor-product representations and consider both Hamiltonian constraints and ansatz-level restrictions for targeting physically valid product states. Finally, we develop grid-value amplitude-encoded versions of both Hamiltonian constructions and compare them with spectral coefficient encoding. Through linear and nonlinear examples, we assess how the choice of Hamiltonian formulation and function representation affects solution recovery, spectral gap, degeneracy, and readout. These results broaden the applicability of ground-state-based quantum differential-equation solvers while clarifying their principal practical trade-offs.
one_liner: Develops alternative effective-Hamiltonian encodings for quantum differential-equation solvers with nonzero constraints and nonlinear cases.
why_it_matters: It maps practical choices in Hamiltonian construction and function encoding to gaps, degeneracies, readout, and solution recovery.
detailed_summary: The paper extends ground-state-based quantum differential-equation solvers by handling multiple nonzero initial, boundary, and data constraints. It compares homogeneous and source-term Hamiltonian formulations, including amplitude-encoded grid values and spectral coefficient encodings. For nonlinear equations, it analyzes spurious ground-state degeneracy from tensor-product representations and discusses constraints or ansatz restrictions to recover physical product solutions.
main_result: The main result is a broader set of effective-Hamiltonian constructions for encoding linear and nonlinear differential equations as ground-state problems.
application_angle: Such encodings are relevant to future quantum simulation workflows for optical, wave, and field equations where boundary data and readout matter.

title: An Operator-Theoretic Model of Entanglement Percolation in Series-Parallel Quantum Networks
abstract: The realization of entanglement distribution (ED) in large-scale quantum networks (QNs), as a fundamental theoretical framework of quantum communication, faces significant challenges. Percolation theory, drawn from statistical physics, has been identified as a potential solution to this problem. Nevertheless, when addressing ED, percolation theory primarily relies on numerical simulations and approximate algorithms. This approach often lacks interpretability and controllability for many phenomena occurring during the ED process in large-scale networks, including emergent phenomena near the threshold. To address these limitations, in this paper, we {focus on} leveraging operator theory to construct a mathematical framework for entanglement percolation in series-parallel QNs. Through the application of operator-theoretic methodologies, we analyze several critical issues within the entanglement percolation process.
one_liner: Builds an operator-theoretic framework for entanglement percolation in series-parallel quantum networks.
why_it_matters: It seeks more interpretable and controllable analysis of entanglement distribution thresholds than simulation-only percolation methods.
detailed_summary: The work formulates entanglement percolation in series-parallel quantum networks using operator-theoretic methods. Its motivation is to replace or complement numerical and approximate percolation approaches with a more structured mathematical model. The framework targets critical phenomena near distribution thresholds and other emergent behavior in large-scale entanglement distribution.
main_result: The paper introduces an operator-theoretic model for analyzing entanglement percolation in structured quantum networks.
application_angle: Better analytical control of percolation could inform scalable quantum repeater and entanglement-routing architectures.

title: Photonic CZ gates based on few-photon scattering from emitter-cavity systems
abstract: In this paper we analyze the performance of photonic CZ gates based on N waveguide-coupled cavities containing two-level emitters. We derive single- and two-photon scattering matrices for one cavity using the input-output formalism of quantum optics and for N>1 cavities using the SLH formalism, allowing us to compute the CZ gate fidelity. We consider two input Gaussian wave packets that are centered on a two-photon transition of the emitter-cavity system, and find a trade-off between optimizing the single-photon and two-photon wave packet shape. While the single-photon wave packet is preserved for large emitter-cavity coupling rates, where there is little overlap with the single-photon transitions, the two-photon wave packet acquires the necessary $π$ phase shift for smaller coupling rates, comparable to the cavity decay rate multiplied by the number of cavities. We find that this trade-off limits the CZ gate fidelity to approximately 60% when averaging over all input states.
one_liner: Analyzes photonic CZ gates from few-photon scattering in waveguide-coupled emitter-cavity arrays and finds a fidelity-limiting trade-off.
why_it_matters: It gives a concrete performance limit for a physically motivated deterministic photonic two-qubit gate architecture.
detailed_summary: The paper derives single- and two-photon scattering matrices for waveguide-coupled cavities containing two-level emitters, using input-output theory for one cavity and SLH formalism for arrays. It studies Gaussian input photons tuned to a two-photon transition and evaluates controlled-Z gate fidelity. The analysis finds competing requirements: strong coupling preserves single-photon packets, while smaller coupling is needed for the two-photon pi phase shift, limiting average fidelity to about 60%.
main_result: The study finds that wave-packet trade-offs cap the average photonic CZ-gate fidelity near 60% for the considered architecture.
application_angle: The result is useful for judging whether scattering-based photonic gates can meet hardware requirements for optical quantum computing.

title: Channeling defect emission through topological Jackiw-Rebbi states in hBN
abstract: When two photonic structures of different topology are joined, an optical mode appears at their junction. Its existence depends only on this topological difference and not on the precise dimensions of either structure. Here we realize the photonic analogue of a Jackiw-Rebbi (JR) state in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) hosting negatively charged boron vacancies, optically addressable spin defects. Two partially etched gratings, in which the order of the radiating and dark band-edge modes is reversed, are joined side by side. Angle-resolved reflectivity and photoluminescence reveal this reversal and a non-dispersive JR state at the junction. The state proves remarkably tolerant: despite fabrication errors of up to 20 nm, its wavelength lies within a 1 nm of the design, as predicted by a systematic numerical tolerance analysis. JR gratings therefore offer a robust, monolithic platform for controlling the emission of luminescent defects.
one_liner: Demonstrates topological Jackiw-Rebbi photonic states in hBN gratings to robustly channel emission from boron-vacancy spin defects.
why_it_matters: It provides a fabrication-tolerant, monolithic route to controlling quantum-defect emission in a solid-state photonic platform.
detailed_summary: The work realizes a photonic analogue of a Jackiw-Rebbi state by joining two partially etched hBN gratings with inverted radiating and dark band-edge order. Angle-resolved reflectivity and photoluminescence reveal the band reversal and a non-dispersive junction state. Numerical tolerance analysis and experiment show strong robustness, with the state remaining within about 1 nm of the design wavelength despite fabrication errors up to 20 nm.
platform_or_system: hBN topological grating with boron-vacancy defects
main_result: The paper demonstrates robust channeling of hBN defect emission through a topological Jackiw-Rebbi junction mode.
application_angle: Robust defect-emission control supports integrated quantum photonics and spin-defect sensing devices less sensitive to fabrication disorder.

title: Tensor Network Simulation of Dynamic Circuits
abstract: Dynamic circuits, which incorporate mid-circuit measurements and classically controlled operations, extend the expressive power of quantum programs and are central to applications such as quantum error correction, state preparation, and distributed quantum algorithms. However, their classical simulation is challenging due to the exponential growth of execution branches induced by mid-circuit measurements. In this work, we develop a tensor network approach for simulating dynamic circuits by extending a DMRG-based method for quantum circuit simulation to support dynamic circuit operations. To address the exponential proliferation of execution branches, we introduce and compare two strategies: a single-path stochastic approach that samples individual measurement outcomes, and a multi-path approach that maintains an ensemble of branches. We benchmark these methods on standard dynamic circuits, including the teleportation protocol and GHZ state preparation, as well as on random dynamic circuits. Our analysis explores the trade-offs between simulation accuracy and computational efficiency. These results provide a practical and scalable framework for the classical simulation of dynamic circuits.
one_liner: Extends DMRG-style tensor-network circuit simulation to dynamic circuits with mid-circuit measurements and classical feed-forward.
why_it_matters: Efficient dynamic-circuit simulation is important for testing error correction, teleportation, state preparation, and distributed protocols.
detailed_summary: The paper adapts a DMRG-based tensor-network simulator to quantum circuits with mid-circuit measurements and classically controlled operations. It addresses branching from measurement outcomes using two strategies: stochastic single-path sampling and ensemble-based multi-path simulation. Benchmarks include teleportation, GHZ preparation, and random dynamic circuits, with accuracy-efficiency trade-offs analyzed across methods.
main_result: The work provides a scalable tensor-network framework for simulating dynamic quantum circuits with measurement-conditioned control.
application_angle: This helps developers and hardware teams prototype protocols needed for error correction, networking, and distributed quantum computation.

title: A Cryogenic Penning Trap Based on Permanent Magnets
abstract: We report on a Penning trap based on NdFeB permanent magnets operated at 4\,K with a magnetic field strength of 280\,mT. Reliable loading and confinement of protons, H$_2^+$ ions, and electrons was demonstrated with non-destructive single-particle detection sensitivity of protons and H$_2^+$ ions using superconducting image-current circuits. The axial frequency of individual particles reaches a shot-to-shot stability of 47 parts-per-billion comparable to that of state-of-the-art precision Penning-trap experiments. Measurements of the proton modified-cyclotron frequency show a shot-to-shot scatter of $0.14$ parts per million (p.p.m.), presently limited by millikelvin-level temperature fluctuations of the permanent-magnet assembly. We outline a route towards improving this performance by more than an order of magnitude. This development offers broad potential for axial-mode-related precision measurements and cost-efficient Penning-trap experiments, and represents an important step towards compact, scalable, and transportable antiproton-trap systems.
one_liner: A 4 K permanent-magnet Penning trap confines single charged particles with superconducting image-current readout.
why_it_matters: It points toward cheaper, compact, and transportable precision traps, including future scalable antiproton-trap systems.
detailed_summary: The work demonstrates a Penning trap using NdFeB permanent magnets at 4 K, producing a 280 mT field. The system reliably loads and confines protons, H2+ ions, and electrons, with non-destructive single-particle sensitivity for protons and H2+ via superconducting image-current circuits. Axial frequencies reach 47 ppb shot-to-shot stability, while modified-cyclotron measurements show 0.14 ppm scatter limited by millikelvin magnet-temperature fluctuations.
main_result: The authors demonstrate stable confinement and non-destructive single-particle detection in a compact permanent-magnet Penning trap.
application_angle: The approach could reduce size and cost for precision Penning-trap experiments and enable transportable charged-particle or antiproton traps.

title: Quantum Chemistry in a Novel Hybrid Dipolar Atom-Ion Mixture
abstract: Merging trapped ions with cold atomic clouds offers intriguing prospects for quantum chemistry and many-body quantum simulations. Especially when going beyond the standard alkali atomic baths by using lanthanide atoms, opportunities arise to study the interplay between the intermediate-range atom-ion interaction and the tunable long-range dipolar atom-atom interactions. However, the high total angular momentum of the ground-state of open-shell lanthanides, e.g. $^{5}I_{8}$ for dysprosium, affects the atom-ion potential. Here, we discuss the implications for long- and short-range atom-ion interactions and present a novel apparatus which combines an ytterbium ion (Yb$^{+}$) with dipolar dysprosium (Dy) atoms. We highlight the consequences of this novel Dy-Yb$^{+}$ mixture for observing buffer gas cooling, (non-) radiative charge transfer, and three-body recombination. While the energy-averaged rates are dominated by radiative charge transfer, particularly radiative association, we find that three-body recombination can compete with molecular-ion formation at Dy densities $n\gtrsim 10^{12}$ cm$^{-3}$. This competition is further enhanced by the expected non-thermal distribution of ion energies. These processes could be experimentally characterised through controlled variation of the atom-ion interaction parameters, providing a direct test of our theoretical predictions.
one_liner: A hybrid Yb+ ion and dipolar Dy atom platform is proposed for probing cold atom-ion quantum chemistry.
why_it_matters: The mixture adds long-range dipolar atomic interactions to atom-ion physics, opening richer tests of molecular-ion formation and loss channels.
detailed_summary: The paper analyzes a new apparatus combining a trapped Yb+ ion with cold dysprosium atoms, whose open-shell angular momentum modifies atom-ion potentials. It predicts buffer-gas cooling, radiative and non-radiative charge transfer, and three-body recombination behavior in this hybrid dipolar system. Radiative association dominates energy-averaged rates, but three-body recombination can compete at Dy densities above about 10^12 cm^-3, especially with non-thermal ion energies.
platform_or_system: Yb+ ion in ultracold Dy gas
main_result: The authors establish expected reaction channels and operating regimes for a dipolar lanthanide atom-ion quantum-chemistry platform.
application_angle: Such controlled mixtures can benchmark atom-ion collision theory and support quantum simulation hardware with tunable long-range interactions.

title: Power-resolved ergotropy and correlation redistribution in a bosonic quantum battery driven by a coherent-state superposition
abstract: Ergotropic-gap relations provide thermodynamic witnesses of quantum correlations, but a direct dynamical connection between extractable work and entanglement remains largely unexplored in multipartite non-Gaussian bosonic systems. Here, we establish such a connection for a bosonic quantum battery driven by a coherent-state superposition. Despite the infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, the dynamics retains a simple structure that allows the relevant work and correlation measures to be obtained exactly. We show that the loss of extractable work associated with the passive part of the battery energy is directly determined by charger-battery entanglement. This relation also separates the charging power into contributions from energy transfer and from changes in the battery spectrum. At the same time, multipartite correlations are progressively redistributed from charger-involving correlations to correlations internal to the battery. For a symmetric resonant protocol, complete energy transfer coincides with charger-battery disentanglement and fully extractable stored energy, while multipartite correlations within the battery are maximal. Individual cells, however, remain mixed, revealing a distinction between global and local work extraction. We further show that, in the regime considered, locally extractable work is entirely supported by energetic coherence. Under single-photon loss, the analytical structure survives, but environmental correlations separate charger disentanglement from maximal work extraction.
one_liner: A non-Gaussian bosonic quantum battery links extractable work loss directly to charger-battery entanglement.
why_it_matters: It gives exact work-correlation relations in an infinite-dimensional battery model, clarifying global versus local work extraction.
detailed_summary: The study treats a bosonic quantum battery driven by a coherent-state superposition and derives exact dynamics for work and correlation measures. It shows that passive-energy work loss is directly determined by charger-battery entanglement, while charging power separates into energy-transfer and spectral-change terms. In a symmetric resonant protocol, complete energy transfer coincides with charger-battery disentanglement and fully extractable stored energy, though individual cells remain mixed. With single-photon loss, the analytical structure persists but environmental correlations shift the relation between disentanglement and maximal work extraction.
main_result: The paper derives exact dynamical relations between ergotropy, charging power, and multipartite correlations in a bosonic battery.
application_angle: The results inform photonic or bosonic energy-storage protocols where usable work depends on coherence, entanglement, and loss.

title: Preselection-Encoded Weak-Value Interferometry for Optical-Rotation Metrology
abstract: Optical-rotation measurements benefit from increasing probe photon number, but their performance is often limited by detector saturation and technical noise in the optical readout. Here we introduce preselection-encoded weak-value amplification (PeWVA), in which the quantity of interest is encoded into the probe polarization before a downstream weak-value interferometer. This architecture separates the sensing interaction from the postselected readout, enabling tunable local amplification while reducing the optical power delivered to the detector. We show that PeWVA does not create additional Fisher information, but offers a practical advantage when detector dynamic range is limiting. We further analyze coherent stray light and phase fluctuations and show reduced conversion of these perturbations into equivalent rotation errors. Using an $^{87}$Rb $M_x$ atomic magnetometer, we experimentally demonstrate substantially improved magnetic-field readout under detector-constrained conditions using both transimpedance-amplified and avalanche photodiodes. The experiments also confirm reduced susceptibility to vapor-cell-induced stray light and interferometer phase modulation. These results establish PeWVA as a detector-constrained optical readout strategy with enhanced tolerance to representative interferometric perturbations.
one_liner: Preselection-encoded weak-value amplification improves optical-rotation readout when detectors saturate or add technical noise.
why_it_matters: It turns weak-value amplification into a practical detector-range management tool for atomic magnetometry and optical metrology.
detailed_summary: The authors introduce PeWVA, where the rotation signal is encoded in probe polarization before a downstream weak-value interferometer. The method does not increase Fisher information, but it enables tunable local amplification while reducing optical power at the detector. Experiments with an 87Rb Mx atomic magnetometer show improved magnetic-field readout under detector-constrained conditions using transimpedance and avalanche photodiodes. The setup also reduces sensitivity to vapor-cell stray light and interferometer phase modulation.
main_result: The experiment demonstrates detector-constrained magnetic-field readout improvement using preselection-encoded weak-value interferometry.
application_angle: PeWVA can make precision optical-rotation sensors more robust when detector dynamic range, stray light, or phase noise limit performance.

title: Geometric construction of optimal probe states in distributed multiparameter quantum sensing
abstract: The choice of probe state is essential to achieving ultimate precision in quantum metrology. For a single parameter, an equal superposition of eigenstates associated with the largest and smallest generator eigenvalues is optimal. This simple construction does not directly extend to multiple parameters, since different parameters can favor different probes. We address this difficulty through a geometric construction of optimal probes for multiparameter estimation in distributed quantum sensing. In this setting, the generators commute and share a common eigenbasis, so each common eigenstate defines a vector of generator eigenvalues. We show that the minimal enclosing balls and ellipsoids of these vectors determine the maximal total quantum Fisher information and the minimum weighted covariance, respectively. In both cases, the boundary of the convex body identifies the common eigenstates that can contribute to an optimal probe, and its center and shape specify the conditions that their populations must satisfy. Our results provide a systematic approach to designing optimal probe states, linking the structure of the parameter generators directly to the attainable precision in multiparameter quantum metrology.
one_liner: A geometric recipe identifies optimal probe states for distributed multiparameter quantum sensing with commuting generators.
why_it_matters: It converts multiparameter probe design into a convex-geometry problem, making optimal-state construction more systematic.
detailed_summary: The paper addresses optimal probe-state selection for distributed multiparameter sensing when all generators commute and share an eigenbasis. Each common eigenstate maps to a vector of generator eigenvalues, and minimal enclosing balls determine maximal total quantum Fisher information. Minimal enclosing ellipsoids similarly determine weighted covariance bounds, with boundary points identifying candidate eigenstates for optimal probes. The construction links generator geometry directly to achievable precision and population constraints.
main_result: The authors give a geometric construction of optimal multiparameter probe states using enclosing balls and ellipsoids of generator spectra.
application_angle: The framework can guide practical probe design for networked sensors estimating several fields, phases, or gradients at once.

title: Error Correction Properties of Covariant Bosonic Encodings
abstract: Bosonic codes offer a promising approach towards hardware-efficient fault tolerance, with many leading examples such as the cat-code and the GKP code organized by an underlying symmetry. We build on a representation-theoretic framework of quantum error correction to formalize the construction and analysis of multimode symmetric bosonic codes, focusing on finite groups. Here, a physical, logical representation and an initial seed state together define the codewords via a covariant encoding. A central observation is that QEC matrices can be viewed as morphisms of group representations, so that Schur's lemma forces entire irreducible representations blocks to vanish. We recover several known single- and two-mode bosonic codes and build and analyze the error protection capabilities of three codes based on finite subgroups of SU(2). We analyze the impact of reducibility of the logical representation and optimize the seed state using the near-optimal fidelity.
one_liner: A representation-theoretic framework analyzes covariant multimode bosonic codes built from finite-group symmetries.
why_it_matters: It systematizes symmetry-based bosonic error correction, a key route to hardware-efficient protected qubits.
detailed_summary: The paper formalizes multimode symmetric bosonic code construction using finite-group representations, a logical representation, and a seed state. It shows that QEC matrices act as morphisms between group representations, so Schur's lemma enforces vanishing of whole irreducible-representation blocks. The framework recovers known one- and two-mode codes and analyzes three additional codes based on finite subgroups of SU(2). It also studies reducible logical representations and seed-state optimization using near-optimal fidelity.
main_result: The authors provide a finite-group covariant encoding framework and use it to evaluate error-protection properties of bosonic codes.
application_angle: The method can help design hardware-efficient bosonic qubits with symmetry-structured protection for fault-tolerant quantum processors.

title: Fluctuation-Driven Nonlinear Amplification of Quantum Statistics
abstract: Photon statistics have moved to the forefront of modern optics, as intensity fluctuations and correlations shape multiphoton interactions and reveal information beyond mean-intensity measurements. Developing high-quality photon sources with pronounced correlations is a fundamental necessity in these fields. Here we demonstrate fluctuation-driven nonlinear statistical amplification of quantum light in spontaneous four-wave mixing using filtered amplified spontaneous emission (ASE). Extending the coherent-pump framework to fluctuating fields, we show how nonlinear weighting of pump intensity combines with bosonic bunching to amplify quantum statistics and reshape temporal correlations. In a SiN microring, ASE pumping increases the zero-delay unconditional second-order correlation from 2.01 to 7.58 and extends the Hanbury Brown--Twiss correlation time by a factor of approximately 2.4. The super-bunched quantum source nevertheless retains heralded single-photon behaviour with $g_H^{(2)}(0)\simeq0.04$, while the same ASE pump supports time--energy entanglement in a silicon waveguide with a raw Franson visibility of 89.84\%. These results establish driving-field statistics as a design dimension for quantum light, broadening the horizons for research into higher-order correlations and nonlinear physics.
one_liner: ASE-pumped nonlinear optics amplifies photon-number fluctuations while preserving heralded single-photon and entangled-pair behavior.
why_it_matters: It treats pump-field statistics as an engineering knob for quantum-light sources, not just a noise property to suppress.
detailed_summary: The work extends spontaneous four-wave mixing beyond coherent pumping by using filtered amplified spontaneous emission as a fluctuating drive. In a SiN microring, the nonlinear intensity weighting boosts unconditional g2(0) from 2.01 to 7.58 and lengthens the HBT correlation time by about 2.4x. Despite strong super-bunching, the source keeps heralded single-photon behavior with gH2(0) around 0.04, and ASE pumping also supports time-energy entanglement in a silicon waveguide with 89.84% raw Franson visibility.
platform_or_system: SiN microring and silicon waveguide SFWM
main_result: Demonstrated fluctuation-driven amplification of quantum photon statistics using ASE-pumped four-wave mixing.
application_angle: This could enable quantum-light sources with tunable higher-order correlations for nonlinear optics, metrology, and entanglement generation.

title: Structured detection beyond spatial imaging
abstract: In a point-scanning microscope, detection through a pinhole improves resolution and replacing the pinhole with a detector array provides redundant encoding of the object spectrum, enabling correction of nonidealities in the imaging system or further resolution improvements, for instance. Here, we show that the mathematical principles underlying structured detection are not intrinsically spatial and therefore structured detection may be used for imaging distributions in other physical domains, such as time, frequency, and velocity space. We numerically illustrate this generality by applying structured detection to an electromagnetic distribution in time using four-wave mixing (FWM). The resulting image reconstructions outperform the temporal equivalent of confocal detection, even as the FWM models are made more realistic and shot noise is considered.
one_liner: Structured detection is generalized from spatial microscopy to domains such as time, frequency, and velocity.
why_it_matters: It reframes detector-array redundancy as a domain-independent reconstruction tool for imaging non-spatial physical distributions.
detailed_summary: The paper argues that the mathematics behind structured detection in point-scanning microscopy is not limited to spatial object spectra. It demonstrates the idea numerically for temporal electromagnetic distributions using four-wave mixing as the mapping mechanism. Reconstructions outperform the temporal analogue of confocal detection even with more realistic FWM models and shot noise included.
main_result: Showed numerically that structured detection can improve reconstruction of temporal optical distributions beyond confocal-like detection.
application_angle: The method points toward improved measurement of ultrafast, spectral, or velocity-domain signals without relying solely on conventional imaging geometries.

title: When are bosonic Gaussian states classical to learn?
abstract: A fundamental question in physics is: When does classical behavior emerge from quantum systems? Bosonic Gaussian states provide a natural setting to explore this quantum-classical boundary, as they capture both the classical field behavior and the intrinsic quantum nature of light. Here, we address this problem from a learning-theoretic perspective by asking: When are bosonic Gaussian states classical to learn? That is, under what conditions (if any) can an n-mode bosonic Gaussian state be learned with as few samples, and with operations as simple, as are needed to learn a classical 2n-variate Gaussian distribution? We establish a smooth crossover in learnability governed by the state's thermal fluctuations: - Cold Gaussian states are non-classical to learn: When the covariance matrix satisfies $Σ\le(\frac12+O(\frac1n))I$, i.e. close to the vacuum covariance, tomography under single-copy (i.e., non-entangled) measurements fundamentally requires $Ω(n^3)$ copies, strictly exceeding the sample complexity $Θ(n^2)$ of learning classical Gaussian distributions. We show that this hardness persists even when few-copy entangled measurements are allowed. - Warm Gaussian states are classical to learn: When thermal fluctuations exceed the vacuum noise, parameterized by $Σ\ge(\frac12+ν)I$ for any parameter $ν>0$, we prove that single-copy tomography requires $N=Θ\left(n^2\min(n,1+ν^{-1})\right)$ copies. This bound is tight and is achieved by simple, non-adaptive, unentangled heterodyne measurements. Crucially, for $ν=Ω(1)$, the sample complexity drops to $Θ(n^2)$, matching the classical case. Our results tightly characterize a quantum-to-classical crossover in the learnability of bosonic Gaussian states, reveal a novel connection between fundamental physics and statistical learning theory, and have implications for real-world sensing experiments.
one_liner: Thermal noise sets when bosonic Gaussian states become as sample-efficient to learn as classical Gaussian distributions.
why_it_matters: It gives sensing experiments a quantitative boundary between quantum-limited tomography overhead and classical-like learnability.
detailed_summary: The paper studies the learnability of n-mode bosonic Gaussian states relative to classical 2n-variate Gaussian distributions. Near-vacuum, cold Gaussian states require Omega(n^3) copies under single-copy measurements, exceeding the classical Theta(n^2) scaling, and the hardness persists for limited entangled measurements. Once thermal fluctuations exceed vacuum noise by a constant amount, simple non-adaptive heterodyne measurements recover Theta(n^2) sample complexity.
main_result: Derived tight sample-complexity bounds showing a thermal-noise-driven crossover from quantum-hard to classical-like learning.
application_angle: The results clarify when practical optical sensing and tomography can rely on simple heterodyne data rather than costly quantum measurement strategies.

title: A Syndrome-Extraction Framework for Distributed Lattice Surgery on Arbitrary Rotated Surface-Code Layouts
abstract: Modular quantum computing is a leading candidate for scalable fault tolerant quantum computation. Performing lattice surgery using surface code patches in different modules requires the use of inter-module gates that are noisier than the local gates. Furthermore, the merged layouts during lattice surgery expose multiple directions in which hook errors can propagate to reduce the fault distance. Existing hook-avoiding schedules either increase the syndrome extraction circuit depth, or let link faults propagate into the bulk. We introduce a seam construction that allows splitting arbitrary merged rotated surface code layout into smaller patches with uniform boundaries that could keep their own hook-avoiding N/Z shaped schedule. At the seam we split weight-4 stabilizers into pairs of weight-2 stabilizers that are mediated through a Bell pair and measured within a CNOT depth of 4. We also employ the use of three-qubit $\texttt{CXX}$ gates for parity measurements at the seam to maintain the minimum CNOT depth. Through this seam construction, we confine the elevated link error at the seam, protecting the bulk from higher error rate. We also give a custom detector annotator for such seams that can find the detector space, annotate detectors in the Stim circuits, and ensure that they are suitable to use by matching decoders. We implement our construction for the logical Pauli-$XX$ measurement lattice surgery and a cross-shaped spatial junction and sweep the link error rate from $10$ times to $100$ times a fixed bulk error rate, and show that our construction gives the lowest and most stable logical error rate than the other frameworks compared here.
one_liner: A seam-based syndrome-extraction method protects distributed lattice surgery from high-error inter-module links.
why_it_matters: It targets a central scaling bottleneck for modular fault-tolerant quantum computers: noisy links between QPUs.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces a seam construction for arbitrary merged rotated surface-code layouts in distributed lattice surgery. Weight-4 stabilizers at the seam are split into Bell-pair-mediated weight-2 checks measured at CNOT depth 4, with CXX gates used to maintain shallow parity measurement. Simulations for logical Pauli-XX lattice surgery and a cross-shaped junction show lower and more stable logical error rates as link errors are swept from 10x to 100x the bulk rate.
main_result: Demonstrated a syndrome-extraction framework that confines elevated inter-module link errors to the seam while preserving hook-avoiding schedules.
application_angle: This improves the fault-tolerance prospects of modular quantum processors where interconnects are noisier than local gates.

title: Error Suppression in Distributed Quantum Computing with Heterogeneous-Distance Lattice Surgery
abstract: Distributed quantum computing requires fault-tolerant operations across inter-QPU links that can be substantially noisier than local gates. Uniformly increasing code distance provides additional protection but also enlarges data patches used for local storage and computation. Here, we introduce distributed heterogeneous-distance lattice surgery using an eight-data-patch ancilla-mediated (8-DAM) architecture, which will be useful for near-term quantum devices with less qubit overhead. In this architecture, the central ancilla spanning the inter-QPU boundary is enlarged while the data patches retain distance $d$. The protocol uses traveling stabilizers to suppress hook errors during merge and split operations between these unequal-distance patches. Circuit-level simulations of rotated surface codes at fixed local depolarizing noise show that logical-readout error rates depend only weakly on link noise. The resulting advantage over conventional lattice surgery grows as link errors increase. Comparisons with uniform distance implementations demonstrate comparable logical error suppression with reduced physical-qubit overhead. We also demonstrate how 8-DAM layouts support two simultaneous distributed logical CNOT operations between four logical data qubits using a single enlarged ancilla. At higher link noise, this construction yields lower logical error rates and more stability than two independent distributed logical CNOTs. These results support selective ancilla enlargement as a resource-efficient approach to fault-tolerant distributed quantum computing.
one_liner: Heterogeneous-distance lattice surgery enlarges only the inter-QPU ancilla to suppress distributed-operation errors.
why_it_matters: It offers a resource-conscious route to robust distributed logical gates on near-term modular quantum hardware.
detailed_summary: The work proposes an eight-data-patch ancilla-mediated architecture where the central ancilla crossing the inter-QPU boundary has larger code distance while data patches remain at distance d. Traveling stabilizers suppress hook errors during merge and split operations between unequal-distance patches. Circuit-level rotated-surface-code simulations show logical-readout error rates that depend weakly on link noise and can match uniform-distance protection with fewer physical qubits.
main_result: Showed selective ancilla enlargement can suppress link-noise-induced logical errors with lower qubit overhead than uniform distance increases.
application_angle: The approach is relevant for modular QPU designs needing reliable distributed CNOTs without expanding every logical patch.

title: Bosonic Error Correction with Fluxonium
abstract: Bosonic quantum error correction (QEC) offers a hardware-efficient route to fault-tolerant quantum computing. To date, however, superconducting circuit implementations of bosonic codes have utilized centimeter-scale 3D microwave cavities controlled by fixed-frequency transmon qubits, with logical lifetimes limited by transmon bit-flip errors. Here, we realize bosonic QEC in a fully planar architecture by pairing a heavy fluxonium, whose $451 \pm 70~μ\mathrm{s}$ bit-flip lifetime exceeds that of any control qubit in previous demonstrations, with an on-chip Archimedean spiral resonator several orders of magnitude smaller in mode volume than prior 3D cavities. We prepare finite-energy Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states and stabilize them using measurement-free error correction with rapid fluxonium reset, extending the logical lifetime by a factor of $1.59 \pm 0.05$. These results provide the first demonstration of resonator control using a weakly coupled fluxonium and, with it, the first realization of standalone bosonic QEC in a fully planar superconducting circuit architecture.
one_liner: A planar fluxonium-resonator device realizes standalone bosonic QEC with stabilized finite-energy GKP states.
why_it_matters: It moves bosonic error correction from bulky 3D cavities toward compact planar superconducting hardware with long-lived control qubits.
detailed_summary: The experiment pairs a heavy fluxonium control qubit with an on-chip Archimedean spiral resonator, replacing the usual 3D cavity and transmon combination. The fluxonium has a reported bit-flip lifetime of 451 +/- 70 us, reducing a key control-qubit error channel. The team prepares finite-energy GKP states and applies measurement-free error correction with rapid fluxonium reset, extending logical lifetime by 1.59 +/- 0.05.
main_result: Demonstrated standalone bosonic QEC in a fully planar superconducting circuit using fluxonium control of a compact resonator.
application_angle: Compact planar bosonic QEC could make protected microwave memories and fault-tolerant superconducting modules easier to integrate and scale.

title: Deterministic photon waveform adaptation for quantum connectivity
abstract: The scalability of quantum technologies will depend on the ability to interconnect independent quantum systems through photonic channels. However, heterogeneous quantum platforms emit and absorb photons with widely differing properties, severely limiting inter-node interference and modular connectivity. Here we demonstrate a cold-atom optical quantum memory that simultaneously achieves near-unity storage-and-retrieval efficiency and deterministic temporal adaptation of single photons between arbitrary and programmable input and output pulse waveforms. Operating at high optical depth and within a fully integrated architecture, the system can store photons with durations spanning over three orders of magnitude and reshape them arbitrarily without compromising efficiency, achieving compatibility with many current platforms. By augmenting the role of a quantum memory from a passive storage element to an active programmable photonic interface, our results establish a key building block for scalable entanglement-based quantum networks and modular quantum computing architectures.
one_liner: Cold-atom memory reshapes single-photon waveforms deterministically while maintaining near-unity storage and retrieval efficiency.
why_it_matters: Programmable waveform matching could make heterogeneous quantum nodes interfere and connect without redesigning each emitter or absorber.
detailed_summary: The work demonstrates a cold-atom optical quantum memory that stores and retrieves single photons with durations spanning more than three orders of magnitude. During storage, the memory deterministically maps arbitrary programmable input pulse shapes to arbitrary output pulse shapes while preserving high efficiency. This turns the memory into an active photonic interface for matching otherwise incompatible quantum-network nodes.
main_result: The system demonstrates near-unity-efficiency single-photon storage, retrieval, and arbitrary temporal waveform adaptation in an integrated cold-atom architecture.
application_angle: It directly targets quantum-network interoperability, entanglement distribution, and modular quantum computing links between dissimilar hardware platforms.

title: The logical set of Gaussian states under the stabilizer subsystem decomposition
abstract: Universal quantum computation requires non-Gaussianity in continuous-variable systems and non-stabilizerness in discrete-variable systems. Yet, mapping a Gaussian state into the Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill logical subspace can yield a logical qubit with non-stabilizer resources. To understand how the continuous-variable structure determines logical resources, we characterize the image of single-mode Gaussian states under the corresponding extraction channel, known as the stabilizer subsystem decomposition. Specifically, we derive series expressions for the logical Bloch vector and characterize the resulting reachable set, enabling an analytical treatment of the robustness of magic of the logical states. We then turn this geometric framework into a certification tool: by mapping a discrete-variable qubit witness to a continuous-variable squeezing witness, we obtain lower bounds on the squeezing of prepared states. We also show that ensembles of Gaussian states can violate both stabilizer and classical bounds. Violation of the stabilizer bound certifies the relational resource known as "set-magic," while violation of the classical bound enables the certification of cryptographic randomness at moderate squeezing.
one_liner: Gaussian CV states are mapped into GKP logical qubits to characterize reachable magic resources and squeezing witnesses.
why_it_matters: It links experimentally accessible squeezing to logical-qubit resource certification for CV quantum computing and randomness protocols.
detailed_summary: The paper derives series expressions for the logical Bloch vector obtained by applying the stabilizer subsystem decomposition to single-mode Gaussian states. This gives a geometric description of which logical GKP qubit states are reachable and how robust their magic can be. The authors convert discrete-variable qubit witnesses into continuous-variable squeezing witnesses and show that Gaussian ensembles can certify set-magic and cryptographic randomness at moderate squeezing.
main_result: The main result is an analytic reachable-set framework for logical Gaussian-derived GKP states, with witnesses for squeezing, set-magic, and randomness.
application_angle: The framework gives experimental CV platforms a route to certify logical resources needed for fault-tolerant computation and cryptographic randomness generation.

title: Influence of fast and slow laser phase noise on the fidelity of the Mølmer-Sørensen trapped-ion gate
abstract: High-fidelity two-qubit entangling gates are essential for the realization of useful quantum algorithms on quantum processors. The Mølmer-Sørensen (MS) gate has become a common choice for trapped-ion quantum computing due to its resilience to ion temperature and its demonstrated record fidelities. However, the spectral impurity of the driving laser field impacts gate performance, with phase noise influencing the qubit dynamics through mechanisms operating on different timescales. In this work, we present a comprehensive theoretical analysis of laser phase noise in the MS gate, identifying two spectral ranges which influence the gate fidelity the most: "fast" noise at frequencies near the motional mode spectrum, and "slow" noise at frequencies on the order of the inverse gate time. We derive the noise Hamiltonians for two common laser beam geometries and obtain analytical expressions for the average gate error in terms of the laser noise power spectral density and gate parameters. For slowly varying noise spectra, we provide simplified error estimates. In addition, we validate our findings against previously published numerical simulations.
one_liner: A theory of laser phase-noise limits in Mølmer-Sørensen gates separates fast motional noise from slow gate-time noise.
why_it_matters: It gives trapped-ion teams analytic error budgets for laser-noise spectra instead of relying only on full numerical gate simulations.
detailed_summary: The authors analyze how laser phase noise degrades Mølmer-Sørensen two-qubit gates in trapped-ion processors. They identify two dominant spectral regions: fast noise near motional-mode frequencies and slow noise on the inverse-gate-time scale. For two common beam geometries, they derive noise Hamiltonians and analytical average-gate-error formulas in terms of phase-noise power spectral density and gate parameters, then benchmark against prior simulations.
main_result: The paper provides validated analytic expressions for MS-gate infidelity caused by fast and slow laser phase-noise components.
application_angle: These formulas can guide laser specifications, noise diagnostics, and gate-optimization choices in trapped-ion quantum processors.

title: Temporal Interfaces in Metamaterials with Shape-Varying Inclusions
abstract: Temporal modulation of metamaterials is commonly achieved by varying constituent material properties, while changes in meta-atom geometry offer an additional means of controlling their effective response. Here, we develop an analytical and numerical framework for temporal scattering in metamaterials composed of cylindrical inclusions undergoing abrupt geometric transformations. Changing the radius of circular cylinders modifies the filling fraction and scalar in-plane effective permittivity, enabling temporal reflection, field amplification or attenuation, and frequency conversion. An area-preserving transformation from circular to elliptical cross sections introduces anisotropy, producing angle-dependent temporal scattering and redirecting the energy flow while conserving the wavevector. We derive these effects using effective-medium theory and temporal boundary conditions and compare the predictions with full-wave time-domain simulations. The simulations reproduce the main scattering and temporal-aiming trends, with larger angular deflections than predicted by the quasistatic model at higher permittivity contrasts. This suggests that moving toward the resonant regime may offer opportunities for stronger temporal aiming. These results identify inclusion geometry as a means of controlling wave amplitude, frequency, and energy-flow direction at temporal interfaces.
one_liner: Time-varying metamaterial inclusion geometry enables temporal scattering, frequency conversion, and energy-flow steering.
why_it_matters: Shape modulation adds a new control knob for dynamic photonic media beyond changing material properties alone.
detailed_summary: The paper develops analytical and numerical models for temporal scattering in metamaterials whose cylindrical inclusions abruptly change geometry. Radius changes modify filling fraction and effective permittivity, producing temporal reflection, amplification or attenuation, and frequency conversion. Area-preserving circular-to-elliptical transformations induce anisotropy, causing angle-dependent temporal scattering and redirected energy flow while conserving wavevector; full-wave simulations confirm the main trends.
main_result: The main result is a framework showing that abrupt meta-atom shape changes can control wave amplitude, frequency, and energy-flow direction at temporal interfaces.
application_angle: This could inform dynamically reconfigurable photonic components for frequency conversion, beam steering, and time-varying electromagnetic control.

title: Monolithic Quantum Error Correction in the Presence of Distinguishability
abstract: Quantum error-correcting codes require that the environment cannot distinguish relevant error processes acting on different codewords. In practice, residual Zeeman, Stark, or anharmonic interactions shift the underlying states, making errors distinguishable and weakening the conditions for perfect recovery. We study this effect with an analytically solvable four-level model and a canonical spontaneous-emission noise model for atoms and molecules. Distinguishability raises the effective Kraus rank of the noise channel, lowers the recovered fidelity, and sets an operational checking time that shortens as the frequency separation between the emitted photons increases. We find that rapid syndrome checking suppresses the buildup of distinguishability and quantify how fast one needs to check to restore near-perfect recovery. Error distinguishability is thus a practical limitation of monolithic error correction, and our analysis identifies fast syndrome extraction as a route to mitigating it.
one_liner: A solvable model shows how distinguishable spontaneous-emission errors limit monolithic quantum error correction.
why_it_matters: It pinpoints fast syndrome extraction as a practical requirement when atomic or molecular error channels leak which-path information.
detailed_summary: The study examines how residual Zeeman, Stark, or anharmonic shifts make nominally equivalent error processes distinguishable across codewords. Using an analytically solvable four-level model and spontaneous-emission noise channel, it shows that distinguishability increases effective Kraus rank and reduces recovered fidelity. The analysis defines an operational checking time that shrinks as photon frequency separation grows and quantifies how rapid syndrome checks recover near-ideal performance.
platform_or_system: atomic or molecular monolithic QEC codes
main_result: The paper shows that error distinguishability degrades monolithic QEC but can be mitigated by sufficiently fast syndrome extraction.
application_angle: It provides design guidance for hardware QEC schemes in atoms and molecules where emitted photons or shifted levels reveal error information.

title: Soft decoding for quantum LDPC codes with experimental validation
abstract: The decoder is a critical component of a fault-tolerant quantum computer, computing corrections based on parity-check measurements performed throughout the computation. A soft decoder supplements its output with a confidence score which, when used alongside post-selection, can substantially improve logical performance. We introduce a soft beam search decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes that uses internal decoder data as a confidence metric, removing the need for extra computation. We perform circuit-level simulations of five quantum LDPC codes relevant for superconducting and trapped ion architectures equipped with our global soft decoder and we obtain up to $580\times$ logical-error suppression at a physical error rate of $10^{-3}$ while rejecting only $0.1\%$ of shots. Then, we simulate an error detected measurement, which is a core logical operation of the walking cat architecture, using a streaming version of soft beam decoder and we achieve up to $210\times$ error suppression while increasing the rejection probability by only $0.5$ percentage points. Finally, we revisit recent quantum LDPC code memory experiments on trapped ions, demonstrating that our soft decoder doubles the logical qubit lifetimes at the price of a mean rejection rate of $2.6\%$--$5.6\%$ per syndrome round, bringing all five codes into the beyond-breakeven regime.
one_liner: A soft beam-search decoder boosts quantum LDPC performance and reinterprets trapped-ion memory experiments beyond breakeven.
why_it_matters: Decoder confidence scores enable large logical-error suppression with small shot rejection, a near-term route to better fault-tolerant performance.
detailed_summary: The paper introduces a soft beam-search decoder for quantum LDPC codes that reuses internal decoder information as a confidence score. Circuit-level simulations across five LDPC codes for superconducting and trapped-ion architectures show up to 580x logical-error suppression at physical error rate 1e-3 with only 0.1% shot rejection. A streaming version improves an error-detected measurement for walking-cat architectures, and reanalysis of trapped-ion LDPC memory experiments doubles logical lifetimes with modest per-round rejection.
platform_or_system: quantum LDPC codes on trapped-ion and superconducting architectures
main_result: The main result is soft decoding with confidence-based post-selection that yields up to 580x simulated logical-error suppression and beyond-breakeven reinterpretation of five trapped-ion code memories.
application_angle: It is immediately relevant to fault-tolerant control stacks because decoder-side confidence filtering can improve logical operations without changing hardware.

title: Near-optimal high-rate surgery from linear PCPPs
abstract: A central problem for surgery with quantum Low-Density Parity Check (LDPC) codes is the design of auxiliary systems which measure large sets of logical operators in parallel, while preserving sparsity and fault distance. We introduce a very general method for designing surgery gadgets which are 'high rate', meaning that the number of operators measured in parallel is large in comparison to the size of the auxiliary system. Given an arbitrary initial $[[ n, k, d ]]$ quantum LDPC Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) code, and an arbitrary subcode of size $μ\leq n$ that contains $t \leq k$ logical qubits, the method produces a sparse high-rate surgery gadget with size $μ(\logμ)^{O(\log\log μ)}=μ^{1+o(1)}$ which measures all $t$ logicals in the subcode. The space overhead is asymptotically optimal up to subpolynomial factors, as the lower bound is $Ω(μ)$. This gadget is produced in time polynomial in $μ$. When logical measurement is performed using these surgery gadgets, the phenomenological fault distance is at least $d$ when performed for $d$ rounds. Our main result comes from relating surgery gadgets with relative cosystolic expansion to linear Probabilistically Checkable Proofs of Proximity (PCPPs), which allow a randomised verifier to probabilistically verify the input to a linear circuit, using only oracle access to the input and a claimed proof.
one_liner: Constructs near-optimal sparse surgery gadgets for parallel logical measurements in quantum LDPC CSS codes.
why_it_matters: High-rate low-overhead surgery is a core primitive for scalable fault-tolerant architectures based on quantum LDPC codes.
detailed_summary: The paper gives a general construction of sparse high-rate surgery gadgets for arbitrary quantum LDPC CSS codes and subcodes. For a subcode of size mu containing t logical qubits, the gadget measures all t logicals with size mu(log mu)^{O(log log mu)}, near the Omega(mu) lower bound. The construction is polynomial-time and preserves phenomenological fault distance at least d when run for d rounds.
main_result: The work demonstrates near-linear-overhead parallel logical measurement gadgets with preserved fault distance for LDPC code surgery.
application_angle: This supports lower-overhead logical operations and syndrome-extraction primitives for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Metalens-transparent ultrasound transducer module for extended depth photoacoustic microscopy
abstract: Optical-resolution photoacoustic microscopy (ORPAM) provides label-free optical-absorption contrast at millimeter-scale tissue depths with micrometer-scale lateral resolution. However, its volumetric coverage is limited by the short depth of focus of conventional optical lenses, whereas system miniaturization is constrained by bulky optics and ultrasound transducers. Here, we present an extended-depth ORPAM system that combines an ultra-thin metalens for optical excitation with a planar transparent ultrasound transducer (TUT) for photoacoustic detection. Fabricated from piezoelectric lithium niobate, the chip-scale TUT provides ~80% optical transparency and enables coaxial optical excitation with simultaneous acoustic detection at 14.4 MHz center frequency. This architecture eliminates the need for bulky acousto-optic combiners and large-volume acoustic coupling arrangements between the transducer and imaging target. We evaluate three ultra-thin metalens designs as hyperbolic, quadratic, and extended depth-of-focus (EDOF), which provide effective axial ranges of 0.3, 0.8, and 1.3 mm, respectively, with lateral resolutions of 1.1 micron for hyperbolic, 1.2 micron quadratic lenses, and 1.5 micron for EDOF across the full axial range. Phantom experiments demonstrate improved visualization of multilayered, inclined, volumetrically distributed targets with the EDOF design compared with the two other metalenses. Label-free imaging in awake, head-fixed mice further demonstrates that EDOF provides extended-depth visualization of subcortical microvasculature without being subjected to anesthesia-induced confounds. This chip-scale metalens-TUT architecture provides a foundation for developing compact photoacoustic microscopy systems.
one_liner: Combines an ultra-thin metalens with a transparent LiNbO3 ultrasound transducer for compact extended-depth ORPAM.
why_it_matters: The chip-scale coaxial design improves volumetric photoacoustic imaging while reducing bulky optical and acoustic hardware.
detailed_summary: The system integrates metalens optical excitation with a planar lithium-niobate transparent ultrasound transducer operating at 14.4 MHz and about 80% optical transparency. Three metalens profiles are compared, with the extended-depth-of-focus design reaching a 1.3 mm axial range and about 1.5 micron lateral resolution. Phantom and awake mouse imaging show improved visualization of multilayer and subcortical microvascular structures.
main_result: The authors demonstrate extended-depth optical-resolution photoacoustic imaging using a compact coaxial metalens and transparent transducer module.
application_angle: The architecture is relevant for miniaturized biomedical imaging probes that need label-free vascular contrast over millimeter-scale depths.

title: Programmable Coherent Memory Kernels for Quantum Reservoir Computing in Waveguide QED
abstract: Reservoir computing requires not only long memory, but also memory distributed over the timescales relevant to a given task. In most quantum reservoir computing architectures, however, the memory profile emerges from intrinsic dynamics and cannot be directly engineered. Here we introduce a waveguide-QED quantum reservoir in which coherent memory return is controlled by the coupling geometry. The reservoir consists of a driven Kerr-nonlinear resonator coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide at spatially separated points. An unmeasured propagating field carries information about past inputs and coherently returns it to the resonator after a finite propagation time, forming a non-Markovian feedback channel without intermediate measurement or classical reinjection. Delay-resolved memory benchmarks reveal two complementary functions: waveguide propagation determines when past information returns, whereas Kerr dynamics convert the returned field into nonlinear temporal features accessible through a linear readout. NARMA-$n$ prediction shows that the optimal feedback delay shifts systematically with task order and approximately tracks the explicit input-product lag. These results establish coherent delayed feedback as a mechanism for engineering task-relevant memory in quantum reservoir computing.
one_liner: Proposes a waveguide-QED reservoir where spatially engineered delayed feedback programs coherent memory kernels.
why_it_matters: Task-matched memory is a practical bottleneck for quantum reservoir computing, and this design makes it tunable by geometry.
detailed_summary: The reservoir is a driven Kerr-nonlinear resonator coupled to a one-dimensional waveguide at separated spatial points. An unmeasured propagating field carries past input information and returns after a finite delay, creating coherent non-Markovian feedback. Benchmarks show that propagation sets the memory-return time while Kerr dynamics transform the returned field into nonlinear temporal features for linear readout.
main_result: The work shows programmable coherent delayed feedback that tunes memory profiles and improves task alignment in quantum reservoir computing.
application_angle: Such reservoirs could enable photonic quantum processors tailored for temporal prediction, signal processing, and low-power neuromorphic tasks.

title: Investigation of Widefield NV-Center Magnetic Imaging for Non-Destructive Materials Testing
abstract: Due to progressing miniaturization, material fatigue is expected to gain importance on microscopic scales. Nevertheless, most non-destructive testing techniques are optimized for macroscopic scales. Therefore, new approaches applicable to miniaturized samples need to be explored. High spatial resolution imaging of a material's magnetic stray field enables sensitive detection of microstructural changes due to the local interplay of magnetic properties, strain, and defects. Up to now, this approach has rarely been used for materials testing since high-resolution magnetic sensing is traditionally challenging. Novel quantum sensing techniques offer the potential to close this gap. One of the most prominent quantum sensors, the nitrogen vacancy center in diamond, is investigated for non-destructive testing applications within the scope of this work. An experimental system based on a widefield sensing approach was developed to image magnetic stray field distributions within seconds to minutes over areas up to 1 x 1 $mm^2$. Magnetic sensitivities below 10 $μ$T/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ and a spatial resolution of 1-2 $μ$m were achieved. The technique offers high mechanical stability, which is crucial for non-destructive testing applications. Comparison with magneto-optical Kerr effect measurements showed that the magnetic field maps are strongly correlated with the material's surface domains while containing additional information from deeper inside the sample. Characteristic changes in the magnetic stray field distribution were detected in an electrical steel sample after cyclic loading. A potential marker for early fatigue damage was deduced from the splitting gradient distribution, while 2D Fourier transform analysis provided additional insight.
one_liner: Demonstrates widefield NV-diamond magnetic imaging for micron-scale non-destructive testing of material fatigue.
why_it_matters: It connects quantum magnetic imaging to industrially relevant defect and fatigue diagnostics on miniaturized materials.
detailed_summary: The work develops a widefield NV-center imaging system that maps magnetic stray fields over areas up to 1 x 1 mm2 within seconds to minutes. It achieves sensitivities below 10 microtesla/sqrt(Hz) and spatial resolution of 1-2 microns. Comparisons with Kerr microscopy show correlation with surface magnetic domains, while cyclic loading of electrical steel produces detectable stray-field changes and candidate fatigue markers.
main_result: The authors demonstrate micron-resolution, mechanically stable magnetic imaging suitable for detecting fatigue-related changes in materials.
application_angle: This points toward quantum-sensor-based inspection tools for microstructured components where conventional non-destructive testing lacks resolution.

title: Detecting a large magneto-optical shift in Py/NiO bilayers
abstract: Here, magneto-optical magnetometry measurements on Py/NiO bilayers reveal a pronounced magnetic-field-induced wavelength shift, demonstrating strong magneto-optical coupling in this antiferromagnetic system. A systematic and monotonic spectral shift of up to ~ 400 nm is observed as the applied magnetic field increases, saturating at higher fields. Quantitative analysis shows that the associated magneto-optical energy variation is on the order of 107 eV, comparable to the magnon energy scale in NiO. Owing to the large NiO thickness, the observed effect originates from magnons intrinsic to the antiferromagnetic NiO layer rather than from spin currents injected by the Py underlayer. These results provide direct experimental evidence for magnetic-field control of antiferromagnetic magnon energies via magneto-optical interactions, establishing Py/NiO bilayers as a promising platform for optically probing and manipulating antiferromagnetic spin dynamics.
one_liner: Reports a large magnetic-field-induced magneto-optical wavelength shift in Py/NiO bilayers.
why_it_matters: Large optical shifts tied to antiferromagnetic magnons offer a route to probing and controlling spin dynamics optically.
detailed_summary: Magneto-optical magnetometry on Py/NiO bilayers reveals a monotonic field-induced spectral shift up to about 400 nm that saturates at high field. The inferred energy variation is comparable to the magnon energy scale in NiO. The authors argue that the effect arises from intrinsic NiO magnons rather than spin-current injection from the Py layer.
main_result: The paper demonstrates strong magnetic-field control of magneto-optical response associated with antiferromagnetic magnon energies.
application_angle: The result could support optical readout and manipulation schemes for antiferromagnetic spintronic and magnonic devices.

title: High-power visible laser via injection locking to a photonic integrated circuit optical parametric oscillator
abstract: Kerr photonic integrated circuit optical parametric oscillators (PIC OPOs) provide a promising platform for coherent visible-light generation, offering broad wavelength accessibility and low frequency noise for applications in quantum information processing, precision metrology, spectroscopy, and sensing. However, achieving large fiber-coupled output powers and high conversion efficiency remains challenging, impacting the practical deployment of these sources. Here we demonstrate optical injection locking of a commercially available visible Fabry-Pérot (FP) laser diode to a PIC OPO, realizing a hybrid laser that combines the complementary strengths of nonlinear frequency conversion with those of semiconductor laser technologies. Using 25 $μ$W of injected PIC OPO signal, we generate coherent visible-light at 635 nm with a fiber-coupled output power of $\approx$ 40 mW and side-mode suppression ratio $\gtrsim$ 36.3 dB. The injection-locked FP laser faithfully inherits the low frequency noise characteristics of the PIC OPO signal, achieving a frequency noise floor of 714 Hz$^2$/Hz. We further demonstrate $\gtrsim1$ GHz wide locking bandwidths that enable stable injection locking without active PIC OPO stabilization, together with coarse wavelength tunability over 6 nm while preserving both high output power and spectral purity. Our results establish optical injection locking with nonlinear light sources as a compelling option for coherent, high-power, and wavelength-agile integrated coherent visible sources.
one_liner: Uses injection locking to transfer PIC-OPO coherence into a high-power 635 nm Fabry-Perot diode laser.
why_it_matters: It bridges integrated nonlinear sources and practical visible output powers needed for quantum, sensing, and spectroscopy systems.
detailed_summary: A commercially available visible Fabry-Perot laser diode is optically injection locked using 25 microW of signal from a Kerr PIC optical parametric oscillator. The hybrid source produces about 40 mW fiber-coupled output at 635 nm with side-mode suppression above 36.3 dB and a frequency-noise floor of 714 Hz2/Hz. The system also shows over 1 GHz locking bandwidth and 6 nm coarse wavelength tunability without active PIC-OPO stabilization.
main_result: The authors demonstrate high-power, spectrally pure, low-noise visible output seeded by an integrated Kerr OPO.
application_angle: This is a practical route to compact wavelength-agile visible lasers for quantum hardware, precision metrology, spectroscopy, and sensing.

title: Optimising Cryogenic Wiring for Microwave-frequency Millikelvin Quantum Processors
